title: Cullen Skink
subtitle: Scottish smoked haddock chowder with potato and cream
excerpt: A thick Scottish soup of smoked haddock, potato, and cream. The fish poaches gently in milk, then the flaked flesh goes back into the creamy, potato-thickened broth. It takes 40 minutes and needs no stock.
sourceNotes: Cullen skink takes its name from the town of Cullen on the Moray Firth coast of Scotland. Undyed smoked haddock from the area (Finnan haddie) is the traditional fish; it is cold-smoked and pale gold in colour. F. Marian McNeill, The Scots Kitchen (1929): smoked haddock and potato soup from the north-east coast. The dish is now a standard starter in Scottish hotels and pubs.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the potato base a day ahead and refrigerate. Add the fish and cream when reheating and serve immediately.

glossaryTerms.definition: Haddock that has been cold-smoked after curing in brine. Undyed smoked haddock is pale gold; dyed versions are a brighter yellow. Use undyed for the best flavour and to avoid colouring the soup artificially.

content.text: Cullen skink is a Scottish fish chowder built on

poached in milk, with the smoky poaching liquid becoming the base of the soup. The potato and onion give it body; the cream at the end makes it silky. It is a complete meal in a bowl. Use undyed haddock: the dyed version turns the soup an unpleasant orange.

Put the {{smoked-haddock}} of smoked haddock skin-side down in a wide pan. Pour over {{whole-milk}} of milk and add the bay leaves. Bring slowly to a bare simmer and poach for 8 to 10 minutes until the fish just flakes. Lift the fish out onto a plate. Strain the milk into a jug and discard the bay leaves. Remove the skin and bones, then flake the flesh into large pieces.
Melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 8 minutes until soft. Add {{potato}} of diced potato and stir to coat.

Pour in the strained poaching milk. Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 minutes until the potato is completely tender. Use the back of a spoon to crush some of the potato against the side of the pan to thicken the soup.

Add the cream and the flaked smoked haddock. Warm through over low heat for 3 minutes. Do not boil once the cream is in. Taste: the smoked fish is salty so you may need very little additional salt. Season with black pepper.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with chopped parsley.

rows.fix: Taste before seasoning. If the soup is already salty from the fish, skip the salt entirely and use a little more cream to balance it.

rows.symptom: Soup is thin rather than creamy
rows.cause: Not enough potato crushed to thicken it
rows.fix: Crush more potato against the pan with a spoon, or mash a small ladleful separately and stir it back in.

content.text: Cullen skink comes from the village of Cullen on the north-east coast of Scotland, where cold-smoked Finnan haddock was the local catch. The soup has spread from a regional speciality to a standard dish on Scottish menus. It is most often served as a starter but is filling enough for a light lunch with bread. The name skink comes from the Scots Gaelic word for essence or broth.
